title: Amar Das and Ram Das
hookLine: then Guru Amar Das and Guru Ram Das, who are our help

cards: Most people, at seventy-three, are slowing down. Sikh tradition tells of a man who, at that age, was still carrying water before dawn, every day, for his teacher.
One stormy night, the story goes, he stumbled and fell into a weaver's pit, and the weaver's wife laughed at the homeless old man. Not long after, that old man became the third Guru.

And the young man he would later choose was another servant, an orphan who had sold boiled grain on the street as a boy. Two people the world overlooked. The Ardas names them together, and asks them for something.

teach.h: AMAR DAS, RAM DAS: BE OUR HELP.
teach.b: The Ardas line runs on from Angad: amar daas, raam daasai, hoeen sahai. Amar Das and Ram Das: be our help. Notice that verb.
The Ardas doesn't just remember these two; it asks them to stand by us. Sahai, the helper, is a word we met in the saloks: You alone are the helper.
Guru Amar Das became Guru in 1552, already in his seventies, after years of serving Guru Angad.

teach.h: PEHLE PANGAT: FIRST, THE SHARED FLOOR.
teach.b: He's remembered for making the langar a rule: pehle pangat, phir sangat, first sit in the line and eat, then join the gathering. Rich or poor, high caste or low, everyone sat on the same floor.
Tradition says even the emperor Akbar sat in that line before meeting him.
He organized the growing community into regions with appointed leaders, built a stepped well at Goindwal, and spoke against practices that harmed women, including sati.
Guru Ram Das, born Jetha, was the orphan who sold grain. He came to Goindwal, served in the kitchen, married the Guru's daughter, Bibi Bhani, and became the fourth Guru in 1574.
He founded the town that grew into Amritsar and began the pool at its heart.

teach.h: RAM DAS: A CITY AND THE LAVAN.
teach.b: And he wrote the Lavan, the four verses of every Sikh wedding, sung as the couple walks around the Guru Granth Sahib. So these two names carry a kitchen floor where everyone is equal, a city and a wedding hymn.
That's the pattern the Ardas keeps reminding Sikhs of: the ones who served became the ones who help.

how: In every Ardas Sikhs remember Guru Amar Das and Guru Ram Das and ask them to be their help; Guru Amar Das's langar rule and Guru Ram Das's Lavan are still part of Sikh life.

o: the founder of the city of Amritsar
the Guru who built the Akal Takht
the third Guru, a servant before he led

games.q: Amar Das and Ram Das — tap the pairs.
p: first eat in the line, then gather

s: Guru Amar Das became Guru as a young man
he became Guru in 1552, already in his seventies, after years of service.
tradition says the emperor Akbar sat in the langar line
pehle pangat, phir sangat: everyone ate on the same floor first.
Guru Ram Das founded the town that grew into Amritsar
he founded it and began the pool at its heart.

games.q: you're an emperor and you've come to meet the Guru at Goindwal. what does tradition say happens first?
o: you sit on the floor and eat in the langar line with everyone.
you send gifts and wait outside.
games.why: pehle pangat, phir sangat: first the shared floor, then the meeting. tradition says Akbar sat in the line.

practice: Let the names ride on the in-breath: Amar Das, and an old man with a water pot in the dark; then Ram Das, and a young man stirring a pot in a crowded kitchen, with each out-breath long and empty between them.
If you pray, add the Ardas's own words, hoeen sahai, be our help. If you don't, think of someone whose quiet service you've overlooked.

wordCard.voice: Amar Das. The third Guru, a servant first; the Ardas asks him, hoeen sahai, be our help.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: pangat, the line in which everyone sits to eat in the langar, equal on the floor.

carryVoice: Your line: amar das, ram das. Two servants, and now the Ardas asks them for help. Day six hundred fifteen.
